How quickly a key gets to a result

Source: R/quality.R
keyQuality.Rd

Counts the steps (couplets answered) it takes to reach each result of a key and compares the average with the fewest steps any key could need.

Usage

keyQuality(key, weights = NULL)

Arguments

key

A dimoose key.

weights

How common each taxon is: a numeric vector whose names are the key's results as written in its Taxon column, such as the output of occurrenceWeights(). They need not sum to 1, and names that are not in the key are ignored. Taxa that are missing from it or NA count as 0, with a warning. A vector without names is an error, as is a name that is there twice. NULL (the default) treats all taxa as equally common.

Value

A list with

  • taxa: a data frame with one row per taxon: Taxon, leads (how many terminal leads end in it), steps (mean over those leads), minSteps, maxSteps and weight (its share of the weights, summing to 1);

  • leads: a data frame with one row per terminal lead: Lead (its label, e.g. "7b"), Statement, Choice, Taxon and steps;

  • meanLeadSteps: mean steps over terminal leads;

  • meanTaxonSteps: mean steps over taxa;

  • expectedSteps: mean steps over taxa weighted by weight (the same as meanTaxonSteps without weights);

  • bound: the expected steps of the best possible key to these taxa with these weights and couplets of at most maxLeads leads;

  • efficiency: bound / expectedSteps, above 0 and at most 1 (NA for a key to a single taxon, which needs no steps);

  • entropy: the Shannon entropy of weight, in bits;

  • bitsPerStep: the most a step of this key can tell, on average (1 when every couplet has two leads);

  • capacityUsed: entropy / (bitsPerStep * expectedSteps), at most 1;

  • maxLeads: the number of leads in the key's largest couplet;

  • depth: the longest route to a result, in steps.

Details

A key is a code: each result is spelled by the leads chosen on the way to it. bound is the expected number of steps of the best key there could be for the same taxa and the same weights, among keys whose couplets have no more leads than the largest couplet of this key (maxLeads). It is found by Huffman's construction, which joins the rarest taxa first, so it is a number of steps that a key can really reach: 3 for eight equally common taxa and couplets of two leads, about 3.55 for eleven. No key can do better, however its characters are chosen. efficiency is bound / expectedSteps: 1 for a key that could not be shorter, and lower the more steps the key takes than it would have to. Real keys rarely reach 1, because the characters that would split the taxa evenly may not exist.

When some taxa are met more often than others (weights), a good key asks few questions before reaching the common ones, and the bound takes the weights into account in the same way.

In a key that has a few large couplets among many small ones (a PhyloTree key has couplets of 2 and of 87 leads), the best key is allowed the largest couplet everywhere, so the bound is far below what the key does and efficiency is low. Three more numbers describe such keys without that comparison. entropy is the Shannon entropy of the weights in bits (log2 of the number of taxa when they are equally common): the information a key has to gather. A couplet with k leads can give up to log2(k) bits, and bitsPerStep is the average of that over the steps this key takes (1 for a key of two-lead couplets). capacityUsed is entropy / (bitsPerStep * expectedSteps): the share of the information its couplets could give that the key needs. It is 1 when every couplet splits what reaches it evenly, whatever its size, and it is not a comparison with a shorter key.

Two cases need a rule:

  • A taxon that keys out at several terminal leads counts once: its steps are the mean over its leads, as if its specimens were split evenly among them, and its weight is not multiplied by the number of leads.

  • A couplet reached from several leads (a reticulate key) is counted by its shortest route from the first couplet, so steps is the fewest steps in which a result can be reached. depth is the longest route.

Leads in couplets that cannot be reached from the first couplet, and terminal leads that name no taxon, are left out of the averages.

See also

summary() on a key, which reports the aggregates; occurrenceWeights() for weights from GBIF.

Examples

q <- keyQuality(arachnidaKey())
q$taxa
#>               Taxon leads steps minSteps maxSteps     weight
#> 1           Araneae     1   2.0        2        2 0.09090909
#> 2             Acari     1   2.0        2        2 0.09090909
#> 3        Scorpiones     1   3.0        3        3 0.09090909
#> 4        Palpigradi     1   4.0        4        4 0.09090909
#> 5           Uropygi     1   5.0        5        5 0.09090909
#> 6        Schizomida     2   5.5        5        6 0.09090909
#> 7  Pseudoscorpiones     1   3.0        3        3 0.09090909
#> 8         Solifugae     1   4.0        4        4 0.09090909
#> 9         Amblypygi     1   6.0        6        6 0.09090909
#> 10        Ricinulei     1   6.0        6        6 0.09090909
#> 11        Opiliones     1   6.0        6        6 0.09090909
q$expectedSteps
#> [1] 4.227273
q$bound
#> [1] 3.545455
q$efficiency
#> [1] 0.8387097

# spiders and mites are met far more often than the other orders
common <- c(Araneae = 50, Acari = 40, Opiliones = 5, Scorpiones = 3)
suppressWarnings(keyQuality(arachnidaKey(), common))$expectedSteps
#> [1] 2.234694
